sections.HOOK: Eight point eight million Danes just had their names, addresses, and CPR numbers stolen.
sections.S1_CONTEXT: The Central Person Register confirmed a massive breach, marking one of the largest data leaks in the country's history.
sections.S1_CORE: Hackers exploited a Danish company's legitimate access to pull data on nearly every citizen, specifically targeting sensitive health records alongside basic identification details.
sections.S1_TWIST: Police are investigating, but your data is already in the wild.
sections.S2_HOOK: With that nightmare over, here's a fix for your AI's memory.
sections.S2_CORE: Cloudflare's Web Search API is in beta, letting agents use live internet data instead of stale training cutoffs.
sections.S2_TWIST: It runs through AI Gateway with zero data retention, so your queries stay private.
sections.S3_HOOK: And for the dev crowd, a linker that won't slow you down.
sections.S3_CORE: Mold 3.0 is here, fully rewritten in Rust after years in C++. It's a drop-in replacement for the old version, aiming to become the default Linux linker.

sections.HOOK: Samsung just gave its users a choice: let us train AI on your health data, or we delete it all.
sections.S1_CONTEXT: The company updated its health app terms to require data sharing for AI model training, effective next month.
sections.S1_CORE: Users who decline lose their entire history: heart rate logs, sleep patterns, workout records, all gone. Samsung says the data helps build better health features.
sections.S1_TWIST: There is no export option. Decline and the data vanishes, not to your phone, not to a backup. Just gone.
sections.S2_HOOK: Speaking of platforms making unilateral decisions, Telegram just lost its front door.
sections.S2_CORE: The t.me domain has been suspended, breaking every short link the platform has ever shared. Deep links to channels, bots, and groups all return errors.
sections.S2_TWIST: Telegram says it is working on a fix, but millions of links embedded across the internet are already dead.
sections.S3_HOOK: On a brighter note, the battery problem might have a real solution.
sections.S3_CORE: Japanese researchers developed a method to recover up to ninety percent of lithium from used EV batteries, using a water-based process instead of the acid baths current recyclers rely on.
sections.CTA: Drop a comment if you'd switch to a lithium-recycled battery.

sections.HOOK: PgBouncer just got four times faster, and the trick was embarrassingly simple.
sections.S1_CONTEXT: The team behind PgBouncer published their scaling story after months of production testing at high traffic loads.
sections.S1_CORE: By switching from a single-threaded event loop to a multi-process architecture, they cut tail latency by seventy-five percent while handling four times the connection volume.
sections.S1_TWIST: So the database proxy is now much faster and handles way more connections than before.
sections.S2_HOOK: From databases to runtimes, JavaScript just got a new contender.
sections.S2_CORE: Ant is a new JavaScript runtime built from scratch with a focus on startup time. Cold starts clock in at under two milliseconds, about fifty times faster than Node.
sections.S2_TWIST: That means Ant starts up really quickly compared to other runtimes.
sections.S3_HOOK: And in the world of physics, a resource just got a major refresh.
sections.S3_CORE: The second edition of So You Want to Learn Physics is out, reorganizing the entire self-study roadmap from classical mechanics through quantum field theory.
sections.CTA: Comment with your favorite physics resource.

sections.HOOK: Linux 0.11 just got rewritten in Rust, and yes, it actually boots.
sections.S1_CONTEXT: A developer took Linus Torvalds' original 1991 kernel and translated every line into idiomatic Rust, preserving the exact same behavior.
sections.S1_CORE: The rewrite boots in QEMU, runs the original userspace tools, and passes the same test suite as the C version. No shortcuts, no stubs.
sections.S1_TWIST: The Rust version is actually shorter. Three thousand fewer lines, mostly because Rust's ownership model eliminated manual memory tracking code.
sections.S2_HOOK: From rewriting the past to rethinking the present, Git's most underused command just got a spotlight.
sections.S2_CORE: The git history command lets you search commit messages, diffs, and file contents across your entire repo history in one query. Most developers have never touched it.
sections.S2_TWIST: It found a credentials leak in a five-year-old commit that git log completely missed.
sections.S3_HOOK: And speaking of finding hidden things, here's one from the hardware side.
sections.S3_CORE: Beavis is a replica of the Ultrasound PnP ISA sound card, fully open source. You can build one from the published schematics and hear the same Gravis audio from 1994.
sections.CTA: If you found these stories interesting and want to hear more about tech news every day, make sure you hit that subscribe button and turn on notifications.

sections.HOOK: Apple's own speech recognition just got benchmarked against Whisper. The results are not what you'd expect.
sections.S1_CONTEXT: Apple quietly released SpeechAnalyzer, a new on-device API for real-time speech recognition on iOS and macOS.
sections.S1_CORE: Independent benchmarks show it matches Whisper's accuracy on clean English audio while using sixty percent less memory and running entirely on the Neural Engine.
sections.S1_TWIST: So Apple's new API is just as accurate as Whisper but uses less memory and runs on-device.
sections.S2_HOOK: From on-device AI to on-device gaming, homebrew hardware is having a moment.
sections.S2_CORE: RISCBoy is an open-source portable games console designed from scratch around a custom FPGA, with its own assembler, graphics pipeline, and SDK.
sections.S2_TWIST: The entire design is MIT licensed. Every schematic, every line of HDL, every tool in the chain.
sections.S3_HOOK: And here is another thing that happened.
sections.S3_CORE: Climate.gov was taken offline, but the scientific community had already mirrored the entire dataset. Open data practices saved decades of climate research from disappearing.

sections.HOOK: Nvidia, CoreWeave, and Nebius are lending each other billions. The collateral? GPUs.
sections.S1_CONTEXT: An investigation revealed circular financing deals where GPU cloud companies use hardware as collateral for loans from their own suppliers and partners.
sections.S1_CORE: Nvidia sells GPUs to CoreWeave on credit, CoreWeave pledges those GPUs as collateral for a loan from Nebius, and Nebius uses the loan proceeds to buy more GPUs from Nvidia. The circle closes.
sections.S1_TWIST: If GPU prices drop by even twenty percent, the collateral falls below loan value and the whole chain unwinds at once.
sections.S2_HOOK: From financial engineering to actual engineering, distributed AI just took a strange turn.
sections.S2_CORE: Mesh LLM runs inference across a swarm of consumer devices connected through iroh, a peer-to-peer networking library. No data center needed.
sections.S2_TWIST: The latency is surprisingly good for small models — under 200 milliseconds for seven-billion-parameter inference across three laptops on the same Wi-Fi.
sections.S3_HOOK: And on a completely different scale, a single-board project is punching above its weight.
sections.S3_CORE: Someone built and ran an autoregressive language model on a 6502 processor. The same chip that powered the Apple II is now generating text, one token every four seconds.
sections.CTA: Hit follow for daily tech deep dives.

sections.HOOK: Google Maps just got a serious open-source competitor, and it fits on your phone.
sections.S1_CONTEXT: Valhalla, the routing engine behind OpenStreetMap, released a mobile SDK that runs entirely on-device.
sections.S1_CORE: The SDK handles turn-by-turn navigation, traffic-aware routing, and public transit in a twelve-megabyte package. No server calls, no data collection, no API keys.
sections.S1_TWIST: It already powers navigation in three African countries where mobile data costs more than fuel.
sections.S2_HOOK: From phones to server racks, ARM just took another piece of the data center.
sections.S2_CORE: Ampere's Altra Max processor is now available on all three major clouds. AWS, Azure, and Google all offer 128-core ARM instances at roughly sixty percent of the price of equivalent x86 options.
sections.S2_TWIST: Spotify migrated its entire recommendation engine to ARM instances and cut their compute bill by forty-one percent.
sections.S3_HOOK: And for developers who think databases need to be complicated, think again.
sections.S3_CORE: Litestream now supports read replicas, letting a single SQLite database serve thousands of concurrent readers by streaming write-ahead log frames to S3.

sections.HOOK: The USB-C cable you are using right now might only be giving you a quarter of your charging speed.
sections.S1_CONTEXT: A hardware engineer tested 50 popular USB-C cables from Amazon and found that only 12 met their advertised power delivery specs.
sections.S1_CORE: Most cables labeled as '100W PD' actually delivered between 25 and 60 watts due to undersized conductors, missing e-marker chips, and incorrect resistor values on the CC lines.
sections.S1_TWIST: So many USB-C cables on Amazon don't actually deliver the wattage they advertise on the label.
sections.S2_HOOK: From deceptive cables to deceptive metrics, startup valuations just got a reality check.
sections.S2_CORE: A leaked internal memo from Sequoia Capital warns portfolio companies to stop reporting ARR based on 'letter of intent' revenue. The memo says forty percent of late-stage startups in their portfolio are overstating ARR by thirty to fifty percent.
sections.S2_TWIST: Two unicorns in the memo have already restated their revenue downward, and at least one is facing an SEC inquiry.
sections.S3_HOOK: And on a lighter note, retro computing just got a precision instrument.
sections.S3_CORE: MiSTer FPGA added cycle-accurate Amiga 4000 emulation, including the AGA chipset. Demos that failed on every software emulator now run perfectly.
sections.CTA: If you enjoyed hearing about these stories and want to stay in the loop with the latest tech news and hardware reviews, be sure to smash that follow button and share this with a friend who might find it useful too.

sections.HOOK: A sixteen-year-old just found a faster algorithm for matrix multiplication. The math world is scrambling to verify it.
sections.S1_CONTEXT: A high school student in South Korea posted a preprint claiming to reduce the exponent of matrix multiplication from 2.371 to 2.358.
sections.S1_CORE: If verified, this would be the largest single improvement to the exponent in over two decades. The technique uses a novel tensor decomposition that three separate research groups are currently checking.
sections.S1_TWIST: The practical impact is near zero. Matrix multiplication in production still uses Strassen's algorithm from 1969 because the theoretical improvements only help at matrix sizes larger than the observable universe.
sections.S2_HOOK: From theoretical math to practical hardware, a chip just broke a power efficiency record.
sections.S2_CORE: Tenstorrent's Wormhole chip achieved 340 TOPS per watt on INT8 inference, roughly double the efficiency of Nvidia's H100 on the same MLPerf benchmark.
sections.S2_TWIST: The catch: Wormhole has no training support. It does inference only, which limits it to deployment, not development.
sections.S3_HOOK: And circling back to academia, open access just won a major battle.
sections.S3_CORE: The White House issued a directive requiring all federally funded research to be freely available within 12 months of publication. No more paywalls on taxpayer-funded science.

sections.HOOK: GitHub just made code review faster by making it lazier.
sections.S1_CONTEXT: GitHub Copilot now generates pull request summaries automatically, analyzing the diff and writing a human-readable description of what changed.
sections.S1_CORE: The feature revolutionizes the review process by letting reviewers understand the intent of a change before reading a single line of code. Early data shows review start time dropping by thirty percent.
sections.S1_TWIST: But the summaries hallucinate about five percent of the time, inventing rationale that isn't in the code. GitHub added a confidence score to flag uncertain summaries.
sections.S2_HOOK: From AI-assisted code review to AI-assisted debugging, error messages are getting smarter.
sections.S2_CORE: Sentry 26 uses an LLM to analyze stack traces and suggest likely root causes, ranked by confidence. It checks against similar resolved issues in your project history first.
sections.S2_TWIST: In beta testing, the suggestions were correct sixty-two percent of the time. Wrong suggestions were more misleading than no suggestion at all.
sections.S3_HOOK: And in a world drowning in AI features, one company went the opposite direction.
sections.S3_CORE: Basecamp launched a 'zero AI' marketing campaign, promising that no user data is processed by any machine learning model and no AI features will be added to the product.
sections.CTA: Hit follow for dev tool updates.
